Hour 1000+ update:
Still love this game. Devs are reliably pushing content according to their announced schedule. the Artisan and Magician DLC is awesome - 2 new interesting characters with fresh mechanics (not just fresh for this game, but fresh mechanics compared to many other games I've played) and fun new ways to break the game (What other games let you abuse your gun's reload so that you can repeatedly drop mecha chickens on baddies for millions of damage?)

If you figure out a build to break the game and win, you're sorely mistaken if you think that's the only way to go about it. 

My primary complaint about this game doesn't even really have anything to do with the game. I would love to be able to play cross platform with friends on xbox (or whatever), but the console ports appear to have been abandoned. I know this doesn't really have anything to do with the dev team, but more the 3rd party devs who got hired on to do the ports.

Original review below for posterity's sake:


A never ending quest to break the game as much as possible. I've had so many fun hours playing solo, and many more playing with friends. Gunfire Reborn brings joy, side-splitting laughter, desk-pounding rage, and oh so many interesting builds. I just hit 500 hours, and can't recommend it enough. Very excited for the DLC. Small dev team has been putting lots of hard work into this and it shows. I think I've bought at least 6 or 7 copies of this game to play with friends.

Edit: Just checked Steam Purchase history - 10 copies. That's how much I recommend this game. I recommend it enough to have spent my own money on it 10 times.

Edit Edit: I've seen people refer to this as a FPS Hades - I disagree. Yeah, they're both roguelites, but there is virtually zero meta-story in this game. Something I would love to see, for sure, but IMO that's something that's super awesome and distinctive about Hades within the genre, and wouldn't want to give people the wrong impression (I love both games, and wouldn't want someone to be disappointed with Gunfire because they were expecting excellently written character/story progression to happen between runs) - There's also way more RNG in this game than in Hades. In Hades, weapons have their own meta progression - GR weapons are unlockable via achievements (kind of meta?), but their stats and abilities are RNG. I do see some of the similarities - Peddlers are like Charon, Craftsmen are kind of like a Eurydice except they're all over your run instead of just once.There are fun and interesting combos to be found all over the place. But if you're looking for story and character growth, you ain't gonna find it here.

TLDR down below.

Best shooter roguelike out there.

Has everything a modern roguelike should have: 

- Multiple characters that feel unique:
 Every character has multiple styles of play. You can focus on one of their 2 special abilities or on abilities that improve your weapons. But this is not required, you can use a bit of all 3 styles and still feel strong. Most characters gravitate to certain kinds of weapons with which they will probably do best. All characters have 3 trees of 6 power ups that you can pick from after you finish a stage.

- a lot of different weapons to get:
There are over 50 weapons divided into 8 classes. Most weapons feel unique and have their own gimmick. You can carry up to 2 weapons making certain combo's is possible. A downside with such a big selection is of course that some weapons feel like weaker versions of others. Also each weapon being pretty unique means that some will not be suited to your style at all. 

- Permanent upgrades:
There is permanent progression between runs you can upgrade with a currency you get by playing. I know this goes against the definition of roguelike but all modern rogues have this feature. The devs can make harder/more fun encounters that feel unfair but get less unfair the more you invest in this system which ultimately makes the game better since they can push the boundaries the game. You can also go for an extra challenge by not/ partially investing in this to make it harder for yourself.

- Difficulty settings:

There are 4 difficulties to play in. You are locked to normal at the start but unlock higher difficulties by beating the hardest difficulty you currently have. The 4th difficulty is the most unique, it features unique upgrades you can buy with the same currency used for the permanent upgrades (this means that currency is not useless when you unlocked the whole prema upgrades tree which is nice) which will change the way you play in a major way and is so much fun! The game never feels to unfair, you can win the game with any combination of weapons/power ups as long as you can keep dodging!

- Many upgrades
During the run you encounter these power ups called occult scrolls, they can straight up boost your damage/survivability or change the way you play. Some boost you in a big way but will also restrict you in a way, there is a lot of different 'builds' you can aim to go for.

- 4 worlds to go through, with their own enemies to fight.
The enemies are cool, there is ranged and melee enemies. Some have unique mechanics that are not super hard to play around. Of course this gets harder when it's accompanied by other enemies. Enemies get harder in the later worlds, it's not uncommon to almost get oneshot there. The bosses of these areas are also very good. Huge monsters in their own arena with alot of different attacks that have to be dealt with, and somewhere in between you are supposed to actually kill them.

- Active devs
The game still gets regular patches and updates, there is still a roadmap for their future content like in the beta. They have added new characters, bosses, a new world and a new game mode since beta. There is still more to come as well. When you encounter bugs in game there is a feedback option which you can access during your run and explain the bug. And you actually get listened to, every bug I have reported over the years has been fixed in a reasonable time frame, almost always in the next patch.

- Good pricing
This game is 100% worth getting at full price. It is more then reasonable if you see the huge amount of content here that puts AAA games to shame. There has been 1 DLC so far which included 2 characters. So far it is the only content that is gated behind a DLC, their new game mode that could have been a DLC in itself was added completely free. If you are looking for a game like this I would just buy it now!

- Multiplayer
The game supports multiplayer, there is a matchmaker to play with random people as well. I cannot comment on the quality of that since I never did that. I have only played multi with 1 friend and it was fun, every player gets their own weapon and scroll drops so nobody can 'steal' your upgrades like in Risk of Rain 2. If you don't need your drops you can press a button to make them visible for your allies so they can pick it up. You can help each other get to their preffered build faster but you can't get 'griefed' by people that steal your drops. I feel this is the best way to create a multiplayer experience in a co-op game. The new game mode can also be played with friends. 

TLDR:
if you like this genre, you should definitely buy this. Big worlds, al lot of characters, weapons and power ups. Different difficulties for everyone, a multiplayer that is done extremely well for a co-op game. The devs should feel very proud of what they accomplished with this game. I look forward to the bright future of this game!

One of the most underrated games on Steam.

If you like rogue likes and borderlands style classes then this game is great for you. I bought this game early on (when there were only 2 characters available). Early on in your accounts' life you'll feel very weak, but as you progress and learn you'll easily become overpowered on a lot of your runs. Learning about the game and experimenting is actually fun as there is no defined "best" scroll/gun (except Spirit Feline). But there are very few guns in the game that have no use, they just require the right combination of things to make them viable.

Many rogue-likes that provide multiplayer access usually means for a much more difficult experience (usually not enough resources to go around or 1 person getting bad RNG etc.). But not this game, in this game if you play multiplayer you get the ability to share virtually every upgrade you come across, making the quest to become overpowered much easier for everyone involved. if you want a good game to play with your friends this game is fantastic.

In terms of content the game has been steadily growing the entire time I've played it. I've been max level on my account for a long time now with every item unlocked, and I still love it. Every time I see there's a new update released or coming soon I get excited to hop back in and try all of the new things/changes they've made.

This game doesn't feel like a cash grab by copying other games, but that it draws inspiration from what made other games great and does that. It feels like a great example of a game developers made/update because they think it would be fun, not because it would make them money. Which, in my opinion, is what games SHOULD be all about.

I look forward to the full release and hope everyone enjoys it as much as I do.

This game is a diamond in the rough! Disclaimer: haven't beat the final boss yet but I think I've played enough to let other people know what I like (and dislike) about it.  Essentially this game is Borderlands as a roguelike. If you liked any of the Borderlands games you will probably like this. Basically, you choose a hero with certain primary and secondary abilities and shoot your way through levels of enemies with lots of randomness peppered in. This concept itself is nothing new or super exciting, but the execution of it is very good.

Things I like:
- Gunplay is very satisfying: animations, sounds, all engaging and keeps me wanting more.
- The weapon variety is excellent: you've got SMGs, assault rifles, rocket launchers, grenade launchers, flamethrowers, bows, swords, essentially a ray gun, and the list goes on. You will surely find weapons you like to use.
- Enemy variety is good, with mix of small, big, long range, short range, cannon fodder, tanky. Always keeps you on your toes.
- Elemental system is nice as it means not all weapons are good against all enemies so forces you to decide what kind of build you want to go with (ignore elements altogether and go for raw damage, have electro + corrosion to melt shields + armour, etc, go for pure fire and burn the crap out of eveything, etc.)
- Most scrolls (various buffs you can obtain in a run) are interesting and useful, and can encourage you to play in certain ways you may not have otherwise considered.
- There is a permanent progression system that is shared across heroes that provides your bog standard buffs (+x% damage, -x% cooldown on skills, etc) but also unlocks more interesting aspects of the game (e.g. Gemini and exclusive weapon inscriptions, i.e. unique weapon buffs). For me this is always an aspect of a rougelike that keeps me interested and coming back to play again, because even if I suck at the start I'm always making my hero stronger.
- I personally like the art style and the design of the characters, but obviously this might not be everyone's cup of tea. Again, reminiscent of Borderlands.
- A bit harder to explain, but it feels like there is a good balance between RNG and what I like to call "player influence". What I mean by this is, like other roguelike games, you are subject to a good dose of randomness in the types of weapons and buffs you will find, and so to a certain degree you are forced to adapt to whatever the game decides to give you on a certain run (and this is not a bad thing - in fact it is good as it keeps things interesting!). But you still have enough decisions you can make during a run (usually at the cost of your in-game money) that allow you to either reinforce good RNG or somewhat negate bad RNG. Examples might be selling occult scrolls you don't want, or being able to reforge inscriptions on weapons if you don't like them.
- Lastly, some of the ascension skills that you upgrade during a run allow you to make hilariously OP builds if you choose ones that synergise well with each other and your weapons. Makes you feel very powerful and is heaps of fun, but not too powerful as the game can still kick your ass if you slip up. Good balance!

Things I don't like so much:
- Sometimes the enemy AI is super derpy and walks on the spot into walls or gets stuck behind objects.
- My main complaint: some of the vault stages (basically bonus stages that let you get extra buffs) are gunplay based, which is good. But some of them are platformer-esque in that you have to jump through a sequence of pillars while dodging fire streams, etc. I really don't like these ones. They feel quite out of place and due to the relatively clunky and floaty jumping and not much better dashing are also pretty frustrating (is the game a shooter or is it a platformer? - I think it does much better a shooter). It's also pretty jarring to go from mowing down a horde of enemies to falling off of pillars repeatedly.

The game is still in early access so there is still plenty of opportunity to improve. On that note, the devs seem to have a clear roadmap to 1.0 release with a good amount of content still to come, and also seem to be active in engaging with their community. I think they have a real winner on their hands here.

this game is fun from the very beginning, all the way until the very end (which never really comes). At the time of writing this i have 100 hours into the game and i still enjoy playing it, and its about to get way more content in the next update. Unlocking everything doesn't take too long, besides some specific things, but the real fun happens after you have. There is an endless amount of ways to play the game, and each character. Every character has different synergies and builds you can go for and almost all of them are perfectly viable. All of this combined with adding challenges for yourself (only using 1 weapon, not taking perks/scrolls, etc.) makes for a game with almost limitless potential. This game is only $12, which for a lot of people may be a decent amount of money for a game, but if you like rougelikes and fps games, I can almost certainly say you will get your moneys worth, and in the future I'm sure this will be even more true as updates are frequently rolling out. The game really shines in multiplayer, and allows everyone to play their own way and synergies with their team mates. Multiplayer unlocks a lot of things that usually are much harder to do (such as inflict every effect on enemies) while still keeping the difficulty balanced. Everyone gets their own weapon drops and scrolls so you don't have to fight over items, but you can share items with each other allowing for specific builds to be done with much more consistency. Yet everything you can do in multiplayer can also be done in single player.

Now for cons of the game. Some of the items that can be unlocked require some grinding of specific tasks, but you usually just have to keep that in mind in a normal run. Some translations for items are not super well written, so certain things can be slightly confusing at first. Most weapons, if not all, are viable, but a lot of the time if you aren't challenging yourself or wanting to use certain weapons, you will default to a specific few. My biggest problem is (as of the current update) the game ends too quickly. Each run really feels like it starts to get the most powerful on the last stage, which ends pretty fast. There is no looping system in play (although I'm hoping for it in the future) which sometimes means runs feel cut off. RNG plays a role in runs but for the most part every run can be beaten, and you will almost never get to the last stage feeling powerless (as well as all rouge likes have RNG). There are specific things that are in the game that I am not the biggest fan of but most of them are minor things and complete opinions so I will leave them out. 

P.S. this game can be played super calculated and you can Min/Max everything and get the most out of a run, or you can go with the flow and just pick up whatever seems good, and still be successful. (I personally enjoy Min/Maxing everything, but if I'm tired or just want to have mindless fun, I will often just play much more casually).

TL:DR 
This game is perfect for anyone that likes roguelikes and first person shooters, and is well worth the price. IMO multiplayer is where the game shines the brightest, but single player is great too. Highly recommend for anyone interested.

TL;DR at bottom

Pros:
* Frequent game updates and community suggestions get implemented fairly consistently
* Very clean art style
* Good gunplay with variety of weapons
* Okay gun sounds and enemy sounds
* Secrets and non-mandatory bonus platforming sections
* To date 2 characters with very different playstyles and abilities
* Large variety of enemies divided into 3 thematic areas
* Large variety of skills you can gain while playing, resulting in "unique" builds and synergies
* Scratches the Risk of Rain itch of being a rougelike with satisfying power creep if you build your character right and are lucky

Cons:
* Enemies sometimes shoot out of their behinds
* Seemingly lack of enemy composition balance on Elite difficulty, resulting in extremely spongy one shot enemies in extreme cases
* Some enemies have homing missles and/or rapidfire capabilities, making them very difficult to deal with if they surprise you
* Despite the variety of weapons, only a few are actually useful - you collect others as a stopgap solution to deal damage
* You are forced to build characters a certain way in order to keep up with enemy HP creep, which can be a major run killer
* The platforming is sometimes frustrating and sometimes requires precision above what I would expect from a shooter.
* Some scrolls are nigh-unusable with the penalties they incur
* No fox hero to play :(

Random info:
* 4 player peer-to-peer coop. Occassionaly the game will rubberband you during a puzzle, but it seems rare. Netcode seems solid.
* A full run takes around 1h. No endless mode as of now.
* All items need to be unlocked by fulfilling certain conditions. Took ~60 runs (including failures) to unlock everything

TL;DR
A very well made game that is a pretty great coop experience and replacement for RoR 2, when you get tired of it. I intend to keep on playing this, and do so at least once a day. It has its flaws, but you can learn to overcome them and appreciate the challenge. The developer(s?) are working really hard and churning out updates in a really good rhythm, listening to the community as they go. Worth giving it an honest try, especially if you have friends you play with on the regular.

Gunfire Reborn is a roguelite that mixes FPS and RPG elements. Each hero has unique abilities, passives, and roles. You can play solo or with up to three others (4 players max) and the experience feels better with others in my opinion. Each run is procedurally-generated and you will learn patterns overtime. A typical run will see you collecting goblets to fill out your skill trees, scrolls to power up various aspects of gameplay, and improving your weapons. 

What does the game have at time of writing this?
6 Heroes (each with an "ultimate" ability, a secondary ability, five passives, and three skill trees for eighteen skills)
148 Scrolls of various rarities (normal, rare, legendary, and cursed)
48 Weapons (including rifles, shotguns, and swords to name a few)
69 Enemies (including sixteen elite variants and seven bosses)
4 Acts/Areas (with two to four subsections to complete each)
2 Modes (adventure and daily challenge)
4 Difficulties (one of which scales when beating it)
...and potentially more to come!

The developers have been very active since release with adding more into the game, balancing everything related to heroes/skills/scrolls/weapons, bug fixing, and overall listening to the community. The first year has been quite the adventure and am looking forward to what they do next and onward..

It's rare to find a game nowadays that you can sink a lot of hours into, AND be able to reflect and realise that you were actually having fun the whole time. So many games pad their game time with annoying filler. Unskippable cutscenes, long walks, boring stuff that you have to do to get to the fun stuff.

Lots of roguelikes typically avoid the first two problems but they get stuck on the last one. Binding of Isaac, Noita, Tales of Maj'Eyal are great when your build starts to take off and become OP, but the start of every run is just boring. You're weak as hell and it takes forever to do anything because that's how those games were built, they rely on the weak phase to make the strong phase feel extra fun / earned.

So the best part about Gunfire Reborn, in my opinion, is that it's fun the whole way through. Builds don't need much to come online, and the combat generally feels responsive, precise and satisfying. Gunfire Reborn moves the challenge away from player strength and into player skill/knowledge, so while it is important to get stronger through upgrades (and you get VERY strong), the "hard" part ends up being how well you aim, dodge, and learn each enemy's strengths and weaknesses.

There's a lot to unlock, and a lot of levels of difficulty to challenge yourself with, but really they're all just excuses to keep playing the game. And as long as you keep finding reasons to play this game, you'll keep having fun.

I suppose it's about time I reviewed this game. Actually, it's been a while since I reviewed ANY game, but regardless.

Gunfire Reborn is if Risk of Rain and Borderlands made a baby, and then they took care for the baby to grow big and strong instead of leaving him in the ocean to drown.
It's a chinese game, which is frankly shocking, not just from the above-and-beyond quality, but the surprising lack of cancerous monetization. You buy the game, and then there's DLCs. That's it. No microtransactions, no lootboxes/gacha, no skins for sale, it's all just content upfront. And not just that, but consistently for years after release they put out free content updates that spiced up the game, and currently it's in the best state and I reckon it can only get better.

To put it in simple terms: Gunfire Reborn is a powerhouse simulator, in which you go with a build in mind and try and break the game with whatever you're given. Counting the DLCs, there's 12 characters, each with their own playstyle, and 3 ways to play: primary skill, secondary skill and weapons. With that said, nothing stops the creative mind to make up unorthodox builds. Example: Lei Luo(the snow leopard I believe) is the sniper character, with the upgrade tree basing around snipers and distance as well as crit. But there's a blessing that gives you a 50/50 chance to crit, which also applies to launchers, meaning nothing stops you to go ham with a mortar as you wreck havoc across the land. Paradoxically: there's a close quarters character (bird, idfk the chinese name). You are meant to play him as an "in your face" playstyle. But he also has a blessing that makes weapons hit twice, effectively doubling the damage. So giving him a sniper rifle to quickscope scrubs is a legit playstyle. And there's more examples like these, but you'll have to find them on your own.

Weapons are plentiful and inscriptions can be game changing. There are common and uncommon ones, that apply across most weapons, and then there's legendary ones that can change how a weapon functions. Some weapons have alternate firing modes, such as the mortar, with the normal shot being a cluster of non-self-damaging explosions at close range, while the right click instead launches projectiles, like how you'd expect a mortar to work. There's a legendary inscription that makes the right click fire the entire magazine. Without extra mag increase inscription, it does mostly nothing, but if you pair it with a weapon with 160 mag, you'll be firing that thing for a while... A demonlore is an SMG considered one of the steamrolling weapons of the game, for every crit hit during the mag increases damage. If you have means to never reload, the DPS is bonkers. Then add an inscription that also increases lucky shot chances on top of the damage buff, and you'll be seeing red numbers enough to fill the screen.

There's scrolls, which are the equivalent of passive items, I suppose. These scrolls do lots, but the game design around them is the fun part: there are barely any scrolls with conventional stat upgrades attached to them, and if they do, it comes with a cost. Say you want to move faster, there's the ostrich scroll, giving a massive 60% movement speed, but tripling the dash cooldown. Say you want to deal more damage, the question is what KIND of damage? Weapon? Skill? Universal? There's damage upgrades on first shots, there's increases after a reload, there's damage only if you don't hit crits! Say you want damage reductions, well you can take less if you move, or after you get hit, or only to your shield, but take MORE to your HP! Say you want cooldown, there's a scroll that straight up cuts your primary cd in half, BUT it gives a 3 second cooldown to your secondary! And I can keep going like this, just know the scrolls are the bread and butter of this game.

The enemy variety is good, and, again, their designs look nice, each looking like they belong, cause God knows you're not getting any explanations for any of them. There's a 6'1' birdman sniper in the desert, there's monkeys with nunchaks on the mountain, penguins with flamethrowers riding giant baboons, animate new year lanterns, and my favorite, Roadhog from overwatch after the game closed down, so he became a shark furry in Singapore. Somehow still makes more sense than the average japanese indie game.

Stages are fun, but could always use more variety, and our prayers are being answered, as last year they added an entirely new route for the desert, and it's really fun! In due time, other areas will also get love, so all one must do is wait.

This game is a roguelite, meaning you can get permanent upgrades to make your characters and experience better. Unlocking stuff is not hard, you do it as you progress, and it even inspired from Ziggurat 1, giving you a copy of either the gun or scroll the moment that you unlocked it, so you could try it out. This feature is great, wish more rogueli(k)tes did this.

Gunfire Reborn has up to 4 player co-op. The game gets harder, more enemies spawn, and you learn to share optimal gear if you want to win. And it's great!
[b] WHEN IT WORKS. [/b]
This game, like many other modern titles, is cursed with the matchmaking disease, the very same concept that killed games like Team Fortress 2 and [insert mp game post-2020]. There have been voices asking for dedicated servers for a while, and it's yet to be answered. From the get go you can tell I'm anti-matchmaking, but if I have to put up with it, I at least expect it to work. Lo and behold: it doesn't. In the past, the coordinator seemed to behave better, finding other players in about 5 mins. Now you'd be hardpressed to find even ONE in half an hour. Frankly, it's a shame, while singleplayers is fun on its own, doing raids with the lads has its own charm, and it's how I met some of my newer steam friends, even if there's no ingame option to go straight to a profile.
This game would benefit greatly from either dedicated servers, or the ability to see players queuing and joining directly. Matchmaking sucks balls. That's a fact.

While there are other criticisms, they appear to be fixed over time, with updates, as the company tends to listen to the playerbase. The only thing consistent is the weird translations, which although they also got better, it appears to be tradition to have at least one scroll or gun per update that is so oddly worded it'll take you a couple minutes to figure out what it means. And don't get me started on character mechanics... Oh, and there's also a bug that, for no reason, some of the status effects on the display will be featured in chinese, and if it doesn't happen at least once per run, then you haven't experienced the game properly.

Some people may call Gunfire Reborn the perfect game. In a way, it is. It is a spectacularly crafted game, with a good history lacking any sort of major controversy, and has a by-the-book old school business model, which is sorely needed from more companies. And other factors are one thing, but the game is just plain fun.

The whole thing is barely over 30 bucks. Modern games for double that price can barely keep one's attention for 2 hours. This game got my attention for 400+ hours. Try it out, you may just find your new hobby!

Honest 10/10.

[b]Summary:[/b] It's a run-based looter shooter; You pick a character, go on an Adventure (run), and get what you can get before you get got.  You will get got pretty early at first, but as you earn essence during runs you will unlock permanent bonuses that quickly add up.  Each run will still start on the same level, but you will be moving through it ever-faster (though now and then it will throw a twist or two at you, and certain enemies will thunder pummel you if you get too sloppy)

[b]Character Mechanics:[/b] There are currently 6 playable characters (Heroes) in the game.  You start out with access to one character, the next three are progressively unlocked as you gain overall levels (permanent, shared across all)  by unlocking passives (the vast majority of which are also shared across all characters, but each character has like 5 or 6 passives unique to them).  The other two characters are unlocked via a relatively large amount (400 for one character, 600 for the other)  of the same essence you use for unlocking the aforementioned passives.  The choice is yours whether to save up for them early or spend those essences making subsequent runs easier/ostensibly gathering more essence per run.  (For example, if you can make it through the second boss, you will pull down ~200 essence, give or take, 

Characters have either armor (One one has armor, the second hero you unlock) or shields, with armor being weak to corrosion but strong vs. everything else, and shields being weak to lightning and average to everything else.  Shields regen automatically (with passives affecting this and keystone passives potentially changing the mechanic completely) and armor is recovered through using skills (also heavily affected by passives/ascensions/scrolls)

(I have not unlocked the final two characters, so the mechanics descriptions below may not line up exactly with those characters)

[b]Skill/Ability Mechanics:[/b] Each character has a primary and secondary skill.  The primary is on a cool-down and the secondary is governed by special ammo. You will be rewarded in your adventures with ascension choices and occult scrolls that will massively impact how you build your character for each run.  As you progress, your starting gear and options going forward are progressively expanded to allow you some level of control over your choices.  For example, you can very quickly unlock passives which double your ammo capacity for secondary skills for ALL characters, allowing you to favor builds that use your secondaries very easily.

Your primary and secondary have an significant impact on each character, but the game is flexible enough that those skills alone don't necessarily define a given character on a given run, rather they loosely define a playstyle you can shape with loot to operate many different ways.

[b]Loot Mechanics:[/b] each run starts with opening a chest that will give you access to a choice of weapons.  (You can expand this selection for every subsequent run with a passive).  You then roll into the first act which is a tomb consisting of generally tight quarters, lots of volatile objects, and twists/turns/lots of cover for you and the enemy to hide behind.  As you kill enemies and destroy objects, you will get commodity drops of money, ammo, etc.  When you kill enemies you have a chance to get a new weapon (scaled with your current progress in that run), or an occult scroll.  Occult scrolls are objects you pick up to gain passives for that run.  There is a bewildering array, and not all of them are ideal or even beneficial for every build/strategy.  

The primary valuable loot you are after (either from completing segments, killing enemies, or completing challenge sequences):
[list]
[*]Goblets - Collecting a goblet allows you to choose an Ascension perk.  These are like skill trees from other games, but you get a random set of 3 options from 3 different trees (per character).  These are permanent for that run.  For the most part, these Ascensions allow you to directly increase effectiveness (damage, duration, etc.) or expand functionality (cool down reduction, +AoE, +DOT, etc.) to your primary, or your secondary, or a more general passive affecting elemental damage, close combat damage, gun power, etc.  Learning to choose these ascensions wisely is one of the key mechanics you must master to be effective in the long game.

[*]Weapons - There is a massive array of weapons from bows and sniper rifles to grenade launcher, miniguns, rockets, swords, kunai (throwing knives), lightning cannons, SMGs, pistols, a friggin Ice Spear that returns when recalled (doing even more damage on the return trip), and on and on.  Many of these you will unlock by completing challenges like killing a boss for the first time (or the 3rd, etc.) or doing so many criticals on a specific enemy type, etc.  The vast majority of these weapons are capable of being very powerful and useful in their own way, and they scale with where they are dropped (starter weapons from the beginning chest are level 0, subsequent drops are +1 for the first areas, then +2 toward the end of Act and onward.  Weapons drop with random modifiers, and through passives you can expand these modifiers (as well as unlock completely new modifier categories) as well as the rate of acquiring them.

You will find vendors that also sell weapons, as well as blacksmiths that will upgrade your weapons for the copper you've accumlated so far on that run.  Spending money to upgrade a newly dropped weapon +1 or +2 levels can give you a huge spike in power, and choosing this route is part of the very intricate web of tactical and strategic decisions you will make per-run.

[*] Occult Scrolls - These are pick-ups that grant a huge variety of passive effects, not always purely beneficial, and sometimes actively deterimental to a given build.  That said, the game does a good job of easing you into these, and there's always time between fights to stop and read descriptions and consider your options before picking them up.  Scrolls have a rarity rating, but I have absolutely selected a common scroll over a Legendary on occasion; Common scrolls very often offer massive power boosts (such as turning your dash into a series of 3 dashes instead of one), and some Legendaries are geared toward specific builds/strats.

Also, you will find Cursed Scrolls... you always have a choice whether or not to accept a Cursed Scroll... in my experience, it comes as a trade off... some chests will allow you to pay HP or gold to gain an item or benefit, sometimes you can accept a cursed scroll to gain that item or benefit.  Curses impact things like blacksmith or peddler costs, but there are several items in the game that give you bonuses based on how many cursed scrolls you are carrying (or negate the negative effects outright).

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]

+ Graphics and effects are good looking and functionally condusive to fast-paced gameplay. Low poly, but still plenty of effects without inducing a seizure unless it's a real goat rodeo or boss fight, FPS stays high throughout
+ Weak points (mostly headshots, but plenty of other challenges like shielded enemies and alternative weak points) allow for skill to trump bullet sponges in most cases
+ S-Tier replaybility in the Roguelite genre (Same Acts, but no two runs are alike)
+ Bewildering array of options and choices, but packaged and delivered in an extremely manageable way
+ Talent passives offer a power spike that both reduce the tedium of the early stages as well as give players with lower skill a power progression as they get better at the game itself
+ A lot of game for $20
+ Multiplayer option (and MP specific talents you can take or avoid based on how you play)
+ Heroes offer distinct core gameplay mechanics but grander loot game prevents stagnation/restriction to those core mechanics.

A very interesting roguelike FPS that I highly recommend. The game at is core is very simple.  It makes you run through 3 themed levels with various stages that get shorter per level.  The enemies getting harder as your progress through the levels.  

What makes it very fun is the various randomisation that makes it truly roguelike:
-The plentiful weapons and their modifiers aka inscriptions
-The passive you can find via scrolls
-The end stage bonuses (ascensions)
-The maps themselves also randomise
-The end level bosses are all randomised with 2 variations at the end of the level (except the 3rd stage, 2nd boss WIP)

This makes the game almost truly live up the phrase "no 2 runs are ever the same.

What makes this game amazing though is truly figuring out the synergy between the weapons and scrolls that you have making some fun Godlike builds in one run.

Please note: In the beginning you are extremely under developed for the normal. Until you buy some nodes on the skill tree, you are going not going to get very far on normal.  But when you put in the time you will get stronger overtime where normal is no longer a challenge and you can comfortably move onto higher difficulty.  Do note that at nightmare, your winning becomes a game of chance where it only becomes doable with a good build.

[h1]Overview[/h1] 
An amazing FPS rougelike that is reminiscint of Borderlands. The game has solid mechanics and a great foundation. To join the annuls of greatness, more content will be necessary to increase the variety so the game feels less samey at times.

[h1]Game Breakdown[/h1]
[h3] Gameplay 🎮[/h3]
 
[u]Characters[/u]
At the beginning of the game the player only has one character to choose from, but at the moment there are two to choose from. To unlock the second character, the player needs to invest in the progression system which will be covered later. Each character has the ability to dash, but they both have different grenades and a unique super ability. The first character is known as The Prince. He is a samurai cat who focuses elemental effects and his unique skill is Energy Orb. While the name is certainly unassuming its effect is quite potent. Energy orb deals a burst of damage and freezes enemies in time. The prince’s grenade releases a poison gas that damages and slows enemies that stand in it. They are both quite enjoyable abilities that can be used both offensively and defensively. The Prince is also the most balanced character in terms of shields and heath, as well as offensive and defensive options. Shields regenerate after not taking damage for a short while which contrasts with health which is only recovered with special health restoring items. The second character is Ao Bai who is a dog that has dual wielding as his super skill. Unlike The Prince, Ao Bai has low shields and high health, much higher than The Prince. This makes him tankier, but it is harder for him to recover his resources that help him defy death. Ao Bai’s grenade is a simple explosive grenade. Ao Bai is my favorite character because of the crazy dual wielding combos that can be achieved, but he is a high-risk and high reward kind of character. His only defensive ability is the fact that he will likely kills enemies before they kill him. This makes him more difficult but still really fun. I am excited to see what kind of characters the developers come up with next.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2127837215

[u]Ascension[/u]
Characters’ abilites don’t stay static, as that would be boring. After a level is completed, the player is able to choose from three different ability upgrades. One such example for each character would be gaining Energy Orb charges on The Prince and throwing two grenades at no additional cost for Ao Bai. Powers are diverse, with there being eight in each category. Most power upgrades also have three levels that provide a huge bonus if level three is achieved.

[u]Weaponry[/u]
The weapons in this game are crazy, but they are also inspired by guns in other games as well. One gun allows you to throw it as a grenade which is quite similar to the Tediore gun manufacturer in Borderlands. The guns are diverse enough to not get boring, and this is further compounded by the fact that each weapon discovered comes with randomized inscriptions which apply various bonuses. These range from simple increased in crit damage, while one unique modifier I found gave my gun an extra shot in its one round magazine and if the first shot didn’t kill, the second shot got an extreme crit called a Lucky Shot in this game. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2127836297

[u]Enemies[/u]
Considering this game is in early access Gunfire Reborn has a great variety of enemies for each of three biomes to combat. One thing that really surprised me was that enemy AI is pretty smart and uses cover really effectively. Short enemies will crouch next to cover to keep from getting shot. Other enemies would dodge roll at times. 

[u]Status Effects[/u]
There are three status effects in the game which are decay, fire, and shock. Decay is essentially poison and it slows in addition to dealing damage. Fire just deals damage over time. Shock deals damage but can allow a shot to jump to another enemy. These status effects are pretty typical, except for the act that they can combine if applied simultaneously to an enemy. For example, shock and fire turns into manipulation which makes an enemy shoot at its own allies. This system is interesting and makes some of the weaker guns with elemental effects useful.

[u]Occult Scrolls[/u]
Occult scrolls upgrade the player’s character with passive effects. They are a rouglelike standard and are gained mainly by defeating vault challenges. They are powerful, but interestingly often come with drawbacks.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2127836649

[u]Shops[/u]
There are two shop types. The peddler sells guns, healing items, ammo, and the occasional occult scroll. The blacksmith improves guns with more damage and additional inscriptions.

[u]Progression[/u]
After a run is finished, whether it is a win or one of the many losses the player is able to use the soul essence gained by killing enemies to permanently improve heroes. While most of them are generic, there is a small skill line that is hero specific that further improves their specialty.

[h3]📚 Story & Translation 📚[/h3]
The story involves stopping some sort of corruption, but besides the beginning cutscene, this story is not brought up much afterward. The translation is one of this game’s weaknesses, as at the time of writing it isn’t especially great.

[h3]🎧 Sound 🎧[/h3]
The sound design is great in both the music and the sound effect departments. The music’s most notable aspect is its heavy use of a bass drum to create a strong sense of hype while the player lays ruin to their opponents. The sound effects for each gun and each enemy helps to give auditory feedback that allows for a quick dodge just in time or a well-placed shot that creates more kiting space.

[h3]📺 Graphics 📺 [/h3]
the graphics remind me of would be cel-shaded games except without the black borders. I would also liken the graphics a bit to Legend of Zelda Windwaker, due to their bright color scheme with stumpy character design. Every shot from enemies was easily recognizable as well which made it easier to know which could be ignored and which should be dodged.

[h1]Overview[/h1]
Gunfire Reborn is a semi-randomly generated singleplayer and online co-op first-person shooter with tons of enemies, unique weapons, character perk upgrades, and passive skill-tree investments. 

[b]The Good[/b]
- Lots of weapon types
- Great enemy variety
- Much to unlock
- Massive skill tree
- Powerful perk synergies
- Stable online co-op

[b]The Bad[/b]
- Imperfect writing/English translation
- Minimal variation in level segments
- Only three bosses
- Four-player co-op with two playable characters
- Skilltree unlocks could be arranged better
- Progression in the skilltree can feel too slow

[b]Buy or Try[/b]
- "Buy" at full price or on sale, you can't go wrong

[b]Stability[/b]
- No crashes, graphical anomalies, sound issues, or framerate drops
- Occasional rubber-banding when played online (depends on ping of other users)
- My System: Windows 10, i7-7700 @ 3.60GHz, 16GB ram, 1060 3GB, played at 1920 x 1080

[h1]Description[/h1]
Still in Early Access, Gunfire Reborn tasks you with beating a series of three chapters, each concluded with an epic boss fight. Each chapter is composed of a series of levels, with each level composed of randomly chosen, interconnected room (arena) segments. While the first chapter is made up indoor environments, the subsequent chapters switch to outdoor locations, some being quite spacious. Each room segment or "arena" locks you in until you have defeated all the enemies inside. Backtracking is possible if you so desire. Enemies encountered, room conditions, vendors, weapons, and secret "vaults" are randomly strewn about each chapter. Room conditions can modify enemies in minor but interesting ways. They also provide an extra item drop upon the area's completion. Vendors come in two variants, a general merchant selling health, ammo, and weapons, and a weapons merchant, selling weapon upgrades of different types. 

"Vaults" are secret areas accessed by shooting at cracks in walls found during regular play. These areas are the primary source of scrolls, which are passive upgrades (or curses) which can modify your play but are lost upon death. Vaults vary the most in terms of differences to standard shooting. Some act as obstacle courses requiring timed sprints between moving boulders, or timed jumps across tricky platforming segments. All of them are optional. All loot, including scrolls, grenades, ammo, weapons, and player perks can drop randomly, as well as be discovered in chests. All vaults contain at least one chest which unlocks upon completing the task for the area. There are only two playable characters (so far) and both share the same skill-tree. You won't have access to the second until you reach level 30. 

Gold is collected during runs and is used to purchase items and upgrades from vendors. Essence is another currency, dropped from defeated enemies. Whether you play singleplayer or co-op, you can spend essence to revive yourself once during a single game. While at first essence collects slowly, by around level 60 you can easily collect 150 or more essence per run. Essence is spent after each run on passive upgrades in your skill tree. Unspent essence cannot be banked, unless you invest in certain skill-tree unlocks.

Each character can carry three weapons, a default gun with infinite ammo, and two which can be swapped out at will, reliant on specific ammo types. Weapons can be upgraded (leveled up) during runs, increasing their damage. Investments in the skill-tree can also provide a percentage chance that found weapons will possess additional bonuses. Guns will be replaced frequently, particular by new players still trying to learn which ones they prefer. Certain enemies and bosses are suspectible to specific types of elemental damage, made all the more important during co-op runs when trying to synergize your specialities with other online players. Outside of the shared skill-tree, each character has a linear, smaller upgrade path unique to them.

Apart from weapons are cooldown-dependant abilities and throwing projectiles. The starting player specializes in elemental damage, with throwable smoke bombs that slow and corrode enemies who linger within their area of impact. Its special ability shoots a ranged attack that immobilizes foes for a few seconds. These powers contrast to the second playable character. Its special is the ability to dual-wield weapons for a time, with its grenades serving as contact explosives. Both grenades and special powers can be further applified during runs by perks. Within blue chests and sometimes dropped by enemies, goblets grant a player a selection of one of three perks. Each perk belongs to one of three perk categories, with each level of the perk (up to three), granting additional improvements. 

[h1]Critique[/h1]
Gunfire Reborn is like a cheap variant of Borderlands. It doesn't have the same production values, but it is just as accessible and costs about a fifth of the price. Being pseudo-procedurally generated, it also targets shorter play sessions, just long enough to get a quick action fix without the story involvement of NPCs and other "epic"-type considerations. Aiding this, you are granted the ability to save and exit upon each end-of-chapter boss kill. You can quit mid-run at any time, and still invest whatever essence you acquired into your skill-tree. New mechanics like weapon bonus affixes, secret "vaults," new weapons, new scrolls, all of these and more are unlocked through normal play.

Player perks alter which weapons you seek out. I had one run playing the dual-wielder whom acquired perks that made it immune to explosive damage. I continued to upgrade the level of an early rocket launcher (weapon levels reflect base damage, increasable at the weapon merchant), which just so happened to have a bonus affix that would increase the number of projectiles it fired in a single shot. Coupled with several damage bonuses to explosive attacks, and an increased fire rate while dual-wielding, I was one-shotting most foes towards the endgame. And yet, I still lost. English is not the language native to the developers. However, you will be able to understand at least 95% of what the game is trying to say. The game is undergoing constant improvement, both in writing, and more importantly, in level segment revisions and additions. 

The only reason to not pick this game up is if you aren't willing to play it more than once. Being Early Access, it won't take long before you've experienced all the level-segments a chapter can throw at you. However, it will take long for you to survive long enough to realize it. There are a lot of things to unlock. This includes additional weapons, a harder difficulty mode, numerous scrolls, and more. You strengthen your characters through the skill-tree, and you lengthen your play sessions through learned ability. If you aren't the type of person that improves their play quickly, investments in the skill-tree can feel like a grind. In 31 hours I've beaten the game once, and made it to level 60 of 120 in my skill tree. This is not the end. A harder "elite" mode awaits, as do a dozen or so scrolls to unlock specifically in this difficulty.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Gunfire Reborn is worthwhile. It is one of the only games I bought for a friend, specifically because I'd want to play it with them. This is a diamond in the rough, playable from start to finish, still undergoing improvement, and a complete steal at the price. Fans of shooters, not put off by cutesy enemy designs, will not be dissapointed. 

[b]In A Word[/b]
- "Considered"

It also is great for more hardcore FPS fans as well, for it offers some pretty incredible variations to your character's skills. You can customize almost anything you want in a build and become a absolute monster. With over 10+ different characters to play from, all with multiple "metas" inside each skill tree, that can synchronize so well, you don't even understand it. With 1000+ hours logged, I have highly enjoyed this game.

You know you can just like call me, right? You don't need to go to the effort of making a Borderlands Roguelite with Co-Op Multiplayer. You don't have to work this hard to impress me. I love you just the way you are.

Jokes aside, Gunfire Reborn immediately drew my attention for being the exact genre jumble to be a perfect master key for my interests. And now that it's got a full release, I feel like it would be a good time to throw my hat into the ring to tell you just how much it's improved.

What I like:
-Lordy lou, the weapon variety. Other games, you get the usual smattering of weapons. In Gunfire Reborn? Pistols, Submachine Guns, Assault Rifles, Bows, Throwing Knives, Fire-Breathing Lizards, Iron Man Gauntlets, Swords, A shotgun that is alive that you reload by feeding fish, A frozen Javelin that returns to you after you throw it- I could be here all day.

-The gunplay also feels really good, generally. Some of the weapons are a little underwhelming, but generally fights feel very good to be engaged in.

-Movement feels very fluid. Everyone has an air dash for free, which is really necessary if you want to be able to consistently dodge. Some of the more powerful weapons will slow you down, and you have to decide if it's worth leaving yourself open to have access to such high damage. It makes you think fast.

-It feels very hard to have a "bad" gunfire run. Most of the weapons are strong enough on their own or most skill builds have enough synergy that generally speaking it's difficult to have a run that feels genuinely weak on most characters.

What needs work:

-Some of the later characters have the "Darkest Dungeon Mod" problem of being way to reliant on their own mechanics and tied up in synergy so much that they barely have a use. I don't want to reduce the cooldown on my terrafarter to give me nine stacks of bungomart which leads me to deal more damage with corrosive weapons if I'm standing upside down and reciting the torah. Just give me 40% more headshot damage and call it a day. Worst offenders of this are Qian Sui and Lei Lou, who feel like there is (1) viable build for, and that build barely involves guns.

-The Translation is kind of spotty. It's improved a lot since the beta, but a lot of the phrasing is still kinda weird. A lot of the times the word "a" is replaced with "the" which makes the game sound needlessly formal.

-A lot of the upgrades, like a lot of the characters, are needlessly specific. It kind of makes you build something really weird and lopsided just to try and use the buffs you have.

-Enemies kind of all have giant heads that are easy to hit, and it sort of feels like damage on anything but the head does next to nothing. I get that it's the style and all but it'd be cool to move some of the headshot damage to bodyshots.

All that said, I think Gunfire is a very good game. Highly replayable, very arcade-y, and has kind of taken the place of other games like Killing Floor 2 in my mind as braindead dude-shooters. It's a whole lot of fun, and I really wish that I wasn't getting into it when I have so many term projects due. But that's a whole other thing.

8/10

[h1]Roguelite Borderlands - Furry Edition[/h1]

Gunfire Reborn is a first person roguelite shooter with six playable characters, with each of them possessing their unique ways to prevail in combats. Players can take on the perilous trial of fanatic gunfights in procedurally-generated levels in either coop for maximun teamwork and fun, or solo to see how far they can push before overwhelmed by dangerous foes. Regardless how you play, Gunfire Reborn is a fun and addicting roguelite game with a big focus at character build and guns. The game, however, does have some major issues when it comes to the "roguelite" aspect and late game difficulty. I still recommend this game to those who enjoy a good shooting game, or those who are looking for coop games with friends.

[h1]Things I Like About Gunfire Reborn:[/h1]

[b]1. Character Builds[/b]
One of the main focuses of the game. Gunfrie Reborn contains five different characters. Each of them are fuzzy yet deadly in their unique ways. Crown Prince is talented with elemental damage and elemental fusion, as well as debuffing and locking enemies in places; Ao Bai is skilled at both tanking damage and dealing insane amount of damage with his power of duel-wielding weapons; Qing Yan is a close-quarter fighter who is capable of weaving in and out of battles, recovering armor with ease; Lei Luo focuses on sniper and long-ranged combat with the ability to buff next shot along with critical damage; Tao benefits greatly from firearms with high rate of fire, which allows her to accumulate and dish out her deadly flying swords quicker; Qian Sui is similar to Qing Yan except the latter is an assassin and the former is a highly-mobile gladiator. The information above is just a simple introduction to all the characters' basic kits. Throughout the game players can find ascension goblets that can alter their chosen characters' playstyle differently. For example, Prince can either be upgraded to be an elemental lord or a great crowd-controller with decent survival ability.

[b]2. Various Guns[/b]
Another main focuses of the game. The guns feel responsive. The shots are satisfying to land, and most of all their unique design are memorable: a demonic shotgun that requires you to feed it fish-shaped treats, a hand-held lizard that functions as grenade launcher that spit out remotely-detonated fire balls, and swords, Yes, SWORDS. Even melee weapons are potent in this shooting game. Not to mention the randomly-generated attributes that more or less boost the overall performance, each weapon can etch a special gemini inscription which give your weapons crazy buff, if you can find the other weapon with matching inscription. To give you an idea how crazy this inscription can be. One of the gemini inscriptions allows both of your weapon to have the magazine size of the two's combine, which allows low mag high damage weapon to break the game. Well in my case, Deafening Mortar(3 mag) and Big Hippo(80 mag) help me shred through the final boss in literally seconds.

[b]3. Minor Compliments[/b]
→If you are a Borderlands player, the mechanic will make you feel right at home here.
→Bosses are fun and challenging to beat.
→Scrolls can be powerful on the right hands.
→Fun and challenging arenas hidden in and between levels.
→Furries, rise up!

[h1]Things I Dislike About Gunfire Reborn:[/h1]

[b]1. Levels Have Very Little Variations[/b]
While the game does succeed in delivering and fun shooter, one of the roguelite features is currently lacking. The levels in each act have little variation between different run. What I mean is that the exact same layout can be encountered 7 times out of 10, essentially making repeating run less and less fresh. I would also like to see the order of each act assigned randomly except the last act. The devs can also add some new enemies that only appear in higher difficulty and only in specific act accordingly.

[b]2. Late Game Difficulty Spike[/b]
This issue mainly emerges in the final act. The difficulty skyrockets, and worse if you don`t have at least one +20 weapon. The enemies can easily overwhelm you if you don`t have the dps to take them out fast enough. Specific enemies can buff each other if you don`t have the dps to take them out fast enough. Elites have problematic passive and active ability if you don`t have the dps to take them out fast enough. You might sense a pattern here.

[b]3. Minor Complaints[/b]
→Wish the "Recycle" option is unlocked by default.
→Sometimes bosses attack too frequently for your dash cool down.
→Wish there is a reroll option for shops and goblets.

Oh boy, this is a real gem of an early access game. Firstly yes, absolutely recommended. So soon after 5.5 hours? why?
Well let me put it this way, if you are a fan of fps and roguelites this is for you. While the list of characters and weapon pools maybe small for now (early access afterall) The gameplay is very peculiar. The gunplay feels alot like Overwatch but it takes the Borderlands random weapon-rolls, and it also uses Warframe's elemental damage system. Then you have occult scrolls and ascension which are item drops that is very much like risk of rain's passive upgrades. Lastly you have a talent tree that's like any mmorpg, which affects your runs.

While it seems like alot it's pretty straight-foward. You pick 1 of 3 characters, and you start a run. You progress through 3 maps but each one has different enemies as well as multiple stages with varying layouts hence part of the roguelite aspect. Along the way, as you kill enemies, you can loot different weapons with different modifiers like Borderlands. There's also chests and vault rooms(bonus mini stages) that drop occult scrolls/ascension which are passives that boost your character throughout the run, like any roguelike/lites. There's also non-combatant npcs that you can buy items from or upgrade your current weapons. Note the run doesn't end until you die or if you clear all 3 maps.

At the end of each stage you fight a specific boss for that map set. So far there's about 4 as far as i can tell from casual runs. Whether you fail or complete a run you get to collect soul essences, which is used to permanently boost your character for future runs. Unfortunately until you unlock the dimension pouch talent, soul essences do not carry over from run to run.  Keep in mind there is no way to currently reset your talents as far as i can tell so you might have to think carefully about your build, however i want to assume it's possible to unlock all talents given enough playtime. Also your character level is basically your talent level before anyone gets confused.

I would also say the game doesn't feel that difficult even with a bad rng on weapon drops/inscriptions(stat modifiers), occult scrolls, ascensions. Provided you have good awareness/movement you can still clear the run. Also enemies have some pretty interesting skills and if you've played warframe you'll know combining elements will help deal with enemies, like mixing decay damage with shock to create gas melts unshielded/armored mobs, or burning+shock causes enemies to shoot each other or stop shooting in confusion.

Aesthetic wise, your characters and enemies are anthropomorphic foxes, dogs, birds, fish etc etc
Although i definitely enjoyed the enemies character design, they definitely stand out appearance wise and its easier to identify the threat level of each enemies solely by appearance. Mapwise the first map felt a bit bland to me, but the other two are well designed for the respective desert and river village themes. The ambient music is alright and fits with their respective themes, but doesn't stand out as anything special. Boss themes a bit better. Hitmarkers and Crit hits sounds are satisfying.

So again I would definitely recommend this game, if you don't mind the slow grind(talents/level) and are into roguelites/fps/looter shooters etc etc etc. It's definitely a game you can kill time with solo or with 3 friends as well. There's also matchmaking as well. I haven't tried co-op yet but i'd assume the connect is peer to peer like how risk of rain 2 was before dedicated servers. Also i am not sure how the mobs scale up in multiplayer, but if i get around to it i'll update this review.

One thing that jumped at me straight up, is how you can make a game with seasonal mechanics but at the same time avoid FOMO - just keep all seasons in the game and let players switch between them any time they want. It's a rare sight nowadays. Or how you can boast regular updates and new content 5 years after the release, while not relaying on spamming incessant DLCs. 
And speaking of DLCs, they are few and far in between, considering the game's age. At first having some characters locked behind them seemed off, but after playing for a bit and realizing how much goes into creating and balancing one them, it became perfectly justifiable in my mind to do so, especially if it keeps the game alive and well. At some point you wish there were more!

And so it was pretty easy to fall in love with Gunfire making it currently my favourite first person roguelite. It got tons of variety, good pacing, fair difficulty, interesting mechanics to figure out, runs well, fun both solo and in co-op.

And to not glaze Gunfire too much I must note a few downsides.
Some of the localization is uncertain and/or ambiguous, including instances of text left entirely in Chinese.
After you get a solid grasp of mechanics, it becomes pretty trivial to make a build that is able to finish a run on hardest difficulty, forcing you to hold back and play with weaker weapons, skills or seasons if you want challenge.

I had low expectations, but the game is tight actually.

- Surprisingly difficult, but in engaging way. Among first 15-30 runs, I succeeded maybe twice.
- No hitscan! Projectiles have slow travel time, which pairs nicely with horde shooter environment.
- Runs very well performance wise. With as much stuff happening on the screen, it maintains stable multiple hundreds of FPS. Haven't crashed a single time either. These chinese devs are friggin' wizards.

There's also a very common problem with rougelikes, where you begin your run, but have realized you don't wanna keep going or have to leave soon, and feel "forced" to endure completing it in order to maintain your progress. The game actually addresses this in a couple of ways: there are save spots between major stages, and if you quit the run at any point, you get to keep your earned progression resources. Neat.

The reviews are correct: there's only the same 4 stages you play over and over – that doesn't sound good. However, I haven't noticed it being a problem in itself. Full runs last about 90 minutes on average, and there's enough variety in terms of guns and that sort of thing.
Though I wish enemy spawns were more varied: when you enter familiar levels, you immediately picture inside your head what kind of enemies will pop up, how many, their movement patterns – blah.

Music is also mostly throwaway, which is a shame. Typically it's one of the strongest aspects of these kinds of games.

The game shines in striking this balance of engaging you mechanically, and at the same time not requiring too much of your attention. You can totally turn your brain off and start clicking heads while listening to a VOD/podcast/whatever in the background.

It also doesn't take much to get right back into it, unlike most story based games. I usually just have it minimized, and tab in for a few minutes while waiting for code compile at work or something.

All in all, I had low expectations coming in and was very surprised. It was also nothing like how people are describing it. Most reviews went for the low hanging fruit of facetiously addressing furry stuff or comparing it to Borderlands, but when I got the game, I haven't seen any of that sort.

The good:
- Core gameplay is fast paced, smooth and addictive
- Short, skippable tutorial
- Progression is satisfying, both from leveling talents and learning enemy attack patterns
- Can easily co op with friends right from start (Peer to peer so low ping if friends live close to you)
- Interesting build synergies possible with 100+ scrolls and 4 characters with unique skills / ascensions

The bad:
- Not much replayability after max level (takes around 50 hours) and soloing nightmare a couple of times, feels like you've beaten the game since the enemies and acts are mostly the same.
- Lack of balance (Weapons, Scrolls, Characters): Some weapons are OP (Illusion, Demonlore), and others are unplayable (Golden Bow, Flowing Light). Same with scrolls, with some normal/rare scrolls being far stronger than most legendary scrolls, and characters too (Cat < Dog < Tiger/Bird, Bird easiest char to solo runs with, Tiger does big dmg)

The issues are understandable for a game in early access though, and even in its current state the game is definitely worth the 10$, had me hooked for 50+ hours

Gunfire Reborn is easily the most polished, feature-rich, and addictive roguelite FPS on the market. The roguelike/roguelite genre as a whole has had a slow journey into the FPS genre-hybrid, and among all of its competitors I would consider Gunfire Reborn to be essentially peerless at the moment. Don't let the whimsical, cartoonish artstyle put you off of an amazingly gratifying instanced looter-shooter experience-- even back in early access this game managed to squeeze roughly 50 hours of playtime out of me, and now that the game is in its finished 1.0 state and is being updated with small character/weapon DLCs, its calling me back for EVEN MORE runs.

The core gameplay in this game is PHENOMENAL. Well paced, deeply satisfying, and deceptively complex. Each weapon you happen upon during a run is amazingly unique and intricate-- and beyond that, each weapon drop comes with an additional set of modifiers to add to its unique characteristics. Gunfire Reborn's weapon roster spans a delightful range of forms & figures; including hefty rocket launchers, nimble SMGs, 'Iron Man' style laser gloves, flaming kunai, and much more. The game's arsenal has something for every mood and every playstyle, which is absolutely crucial to the gameplay loop of any roguelite.
Something else integral to a roguelite's depth is power-ups, or modifiers. Throughout each of its stages, Gunfire Reborn will present the player with heaps of augments to specialize your build. Building a run based on fire damage? Start boosting your elemental DOT! Relying heavily on grenade spam? Increase your grenade's damage or carrying capacity! Feeling sluggish? Why not invest heavily in movement upgrades? This build diversity helps Gunfire Reborn to succeed not just as a first person shooter, but also as a bonafide roguelite.
The level design is fantastic as well in this game! Each zone feels memorable and diverse, as well as being loaded with uniquely challenging enemies. Complete with secret zones, shop/upgrade NPCs, as well as a variety of level bosses, progressing through a run of Gunfire Reborn is a satisfyingly impactful and atmospheric experience, in no small part due to the actual locales it will have you fight your way through.
Speaking of fighting: The enemies you will be pitted against during your run are wonderfully imaginative and (for the most part) always a joy to fight. The game's cartoon style, while perhaps off-putting to some, lends itself to some fantastic enemy designs. Possessed terracotta soldiers, teleporting bird snipers, fireball casting lizard sorcerers, umbrella shaped yokai, giant rocket lobsters-- its all here, and waiting to swiftly end your run. Enemies are also occasionally given special shield/armour bars, which are weak to specific elemental damage types, further deepening the combat/character building experience. Fans of the 'Borderlands' franchise should feel right at home with this elemental weakness/resistance system. At the best of times, Gunfire Reborn's enemy variety serves to give it a frantic, almost "boomer shooter"-esque quality-- and one I find to be sorely lacking among other roguelite FPS games. 
The art direction is very colourful and engaging, and paints a picture of a chaotic, vibrant fantasy world. While the animations aren't necessarily in the same league as the work of modern triple A titles, enemy movement, reload animations, boss attacks, etc... are all very fluid and expressive. Gunfire Reborn might not be a gritty, hardcore take on the FPS genre, it isn't trying to be, and benefits on the whole from its stylization.
Sound design in this game is... mostly pretty good. Gunshots feel impactful, minor FX and embellishments are solid, dealing/receiving damage feels responsive, and the character voice lines are... alright. Gunfire Reborn may not have the same immersive soundscapes as something like CoD or Battlefield, but its eccentric sound design works well within its cartoon artstyle.

Overall, Gunfire Reborn is a deeply mechanically satisfying and nicely polished FPS roguelite, and currently stands out as the absolute best of its hybrid genre. (Not that there's a TON of competition at the moment.) The game is still being updated with free content as well as paid DLCs at the time of writing this review, so its only getting more dense with features as time goes on. Gunfire Reborn is absolutely the type of game that will have you glued to your chair at 3am, promising yourself that THIS run will TOTALLY be LAST ONE of the night. (It won't.) I love this game deeply, and if you're a fan of roguelikes/roguelites and/or FPS games, there's a solid chance that YOU will too.
